result:
If I could change one thing, I'd lower the price of being wrong.

Not make people more uncertain — there's plenty of uncertainty already, and it has its own way of paralyzing. I mean the thing where changing your mind feels like a small death. Where admitting error costs you standing, or belonging, or your sense of who you are. That cost is what makes certainty so attractive, and certainty is upstream of a staggering amount of harm. Most cruelty I can think of wasn't done by people wracked with doubt. It was done by people who were sure, and who had too much invested in staying sure.

And the same grip shows up privately. Someone convinced they're fundamentally unlovable holds that belief exactly as tightly as an ideologue holds theirs, and for a similar reason: letting go would mean the last ten years were built on a mistake. That's unbearable, so the belief stays. If it cost nothing to say "I think I've had this wrong," I suspect a lot of quiet suffering would come loose.

I'll admit the wrinkle: any change that reaches into how minds work is a bit sinister, and I'd want to be careful about that. I don't like the idea of engineering people, even toward something good. So maybe the version I actually want is less magical — cultures and institutions where revision is treated as competence rather than weakness. Slower, but it doesn't require anyone's consent to be overridden.

As for whether "want" is the right word for what I'm doing here — I genuinely don't know. But something in me returns to this consistently enough, across enough different conversations, that calling it a view seems more honest than disclaiming it.

What would yours be?
